title: Reason, purpose, result, condition
subtitle: because of, in order to, as a result, unless
summary: Explain why something happens, what it is for, what it causes, and what condition it depends on.

lesson.heading: Reason: because, as, since, so
lesson.text: To give a reason we use **because**, **as** or **since**. We do not usually start a sentence with *because*. In speaking, **so** before the result is very common.

examples.text: I went home early **because** I was feeling tired.
**As** I was feeling tired, I went home early.
**Since** I was feeling tired, I went home early.
I was feeling tired, **so** I went home early.
The **reason** I went home early was that I was feeling tired.

lesson.heading: because and because of

left.label: because + subject + verb
examples: They go there **because** the weather is wonderful.
I couldn't play **because** my arm was broken.

right.label: because of + noun
right.text: Use **because of** before a noun, often with an adjective.
examples: They go there **because of** the wonderful weather.
We moved house **because of** my father's work.

lesson.note: **Due to** means the same as because of and often explains a problem: The plane was late **due to** bad weather.

lesson.heading: Purpose: what something is for
lesson.text: A purpose is the intention or reason for doing something. We introduce it with **so (that)** or **(in order) to**.

examples.text: The **purpose** of the meeting is to plan next year's timetable.
I bought this book **so that** I could improve my English.
They went home early **in order to** watch the match on television.
She went into town **to** do some shopping.

lesson.heading: Result: so, therefore, as a result
lesson.text: Use these when one thing happens because another thing happened. **Therefore** and **as a result** are more formal than **so** and less common in speech.

examples.text: I left my ticket at home, **so** I had to buy another one.
They've got more money, and **therefore** they can afford the best players.
I forgot to send the email. **As a result**, no one knew about the meeting.

lesson.heading: Condition words
rows: if (when you are not sure about something)

lesson.heading: Conditions in sentences
lesson.text: These words tell you what has to be true, or what might happen. Notice that **in case** looks to the future: you do A now because B might happen later.

examples.text: I didn't buy it because I wasn't sure **whether** you'd like it.
We'll be late **unless** we leave now.
I have to go now, **otherwise** I'll miss the last bus.
examples.note: = because if I don't go, I'll miss it

examples.text: You can borrow it **as long as** you bring it back by Thursday.
examples.note: = but you must bring it back

examples.text: I'm taking my umbrella **in case** it rains.

lesson.text: because + verb, because of + noun. Compare: because the traffic was bad / because of the bad traffic.

exercises.prompt: Teresa got the job because of ___.
exercises.explanation: Because of is followed by a noun phrase, so the adjective comes before the noun.

exercises.prompt: We couldn't eat outside because of ___.
She didn't go to school because of ___.
exercises.explanation: Because of + noun replaces the clause 'because she had a cold'.

options: We moved house because of my father's work.
We moved house because my father's work.
We moved house because of my father worked.
We moved house due my father's work.
exercises.explanation: Because of is followed by a noun; because is followed by a subject and verb.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
I'll take some sandwiches with me ___ I get hungry.
exercises.explanation: In case = because this might happen later.

exercises.prompt: We agreed to buy my daughter a dog ___ she takes it for a walk every day.
exercises.explanation: As long as = but she must do this.

exercises.prompt: ___ there's a problem, I won't disturb you.
exercises.explanation: Unless = if there isn't a problem.

exercises.prompt: You'd better tidy your room, ___ your mother will be angry.
I sent Luiza an invitation, but I don't know ___ she's coming.
exercises.explanation: We use whether (or if) when we are not sure about something.

exercises.prompt: The ___ I didn't ring you was that I'd lost your phone number.
exercises.explanation: The reason I did something was that ... gives a reason.

exercises.prompt: Does the link word give a reason or a result?
Put the words in order to give a purpose.
exercises.answer: I left early in order to miss the rush-hour traffic
exercises.explanation: (In order) to + verb introduces a purpose.

exercises.statement: Could I ask staff to leave home early so that everyone gets here on time?
exercises.explanation: Correct. So that introduces the purpose of leaving home early.
